newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa, EU trade talks within 10 days - source.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa, EU trade talks within 10 days - source.

text.p: Stalled trade talks between South Africa and the European Union could resume in Pretoria within 10 days, a government source said on Friday.
South Africa wanted a speedy resumption of talks after it broke an impasse last month by outlining its negotiating mandate to the EU.
"It is going to be within 10 days," the government source said, adding that the talks would take place in Pretoria.
Department of Trade and Industry director of trade relations Bahle Sibisi said dates were still being finalised but added that Pretoria wanted talks to resume soon.
"South Africa is still interested in ensuring a speedy start to the negotiations," he said.
The EU, which absorbs some 40 percent of South African exports and accounts for more than a third of South African imports, set out its negotiating mandate in March last year.
The EU position was criticised by several influential parties in South Africa as being too harsh on the country and its smaller southern African neighbours.
Brussels has refused post-apartheid South Africa full accession to the Lome Convention which grants favourable access to its markets to developing countries in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.

The EU produced a mandate which would exclude nearly 40 percent of South Africa's agricultural products from a future free trade deal, while calling on it to reduce tariffs to ensure easier access to its markets for European producers.

South African parliamentarians criticised this fiercely, claiming that the EU had failed to take into account the very different sizes and levels of development of the economies of the negotiating partners.
In turn, the EU criticised South Africa for dragging its heels in presenting its own position.
There have also been growing concerns within the southern Africa region about the impact of a free trade deal between Pretoria and Brussels on the economies of some of South Africa's neighbours.
Other members of the five-nation South Africa Customs Union (SACU) -- Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Swaziland -- fear they will lose millions in income from the joint customs revenue pool. REUTER
